title: Write test cases for a payment gateway with a focus on financial correctness and reliability — success, failure, insufficient balance, invalid/expired card, wrong CVV, payment timeout, DUPLICATE payment request, network/callback failure, refund and partial refund, currency conversion, transaction-status mismatch, user closes the browser mid-payment, and the critical case where the payment SUCCEEDS but the confirmation fails — and why do idempotency and duplicate-transaction handling matter more here than UI validation?
shortTitle: Writing payment gateway test cases focused on financial correctness and reliability
topicTitle: Write test cases for a payment gateway with a focus on financial correctness and

s1_definition.profdef: Payment gateway testing focuses on financial correctness and reliability rather than cosmetics, because a mistake moves real money. It covers the success path, declines such as insufficient balance, invalid or expired card, and wrong CVV, reliability failures such as payment timeout, network and callback failures, and the user closing the browser mid-payment, and correctness-critical flows such as duplicate payment requests, refunds and partial refunds, currency conversion, and transaction-status mismatches between the gateway and the merchant. The most important case is the payment succeeding at the gateway while the confirmation back to the merchant fails, which must never result in a double charge or a lost payment. Idempotency and duplicate-transaction handling matter more than UI validation here because retries and network failures are routine, and only an idempotency key and robust reconciliation prevent charging a customer twice.
s1_definition.analogy: When Priya pays fifty thousand rupees through the National Bank of India gateway, the tester cares less about whether the form looks nice and far more about money being exactly right. What if her card is expired, what if the network drops right after the bank charged her but before the shop heard back, what if she double-clicks pay, what if she closes the browser halfway, what if a refund is partial? The scariest case is: the bank really took her money, but the message confirming it got lost, so the shop thinks she did not pay. If the system is not careful, she gets charged twice or the shop ships nothing. The safeguard is an idempotency key, a unique ticket on the request so that even if it is sent five times, the money moves exactly once.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Payment gateway testing focuses on financial correctness and reliability rather than cosmetics, because a mistake moves real money. It covers the success path, declines such as insufficient balance, invalid or expired card, and wrong CVV, reliability failures such as payment timeout, network and callback failures, and the user closing the browser mid-payment, and correctness-critical flows such as duplicate payment requests, refunds and partial refunds, currency conversion, and transaction-status mismatches between the gateway and the merchant. The most important case is the payment succeeding at the gateway while the confirmation back to the merchant fails, which must never result in a double charge or a lost payment. Idempotency and duplicate-transaction handling matter more than UI validation here because retries and network failures are routine, and only an idempotency key and robust reconciliation prevent charging a customer twice.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When Priya pays fifty thousand rupees through the National Bank of India gateway, the tester cares less about whether the form looks nice and far more about money being exactly right. What if her card is expired, what if the network drops right after the bank charged her but before the shop heard back, what if she double-clicks pay, what if she closes the browser halfway, what if a refund is partial? The scariest case is: the bank really took her money, but the message confirming it got lost, so the shop thinks she did not pay. If the system is not careful, she gets charged twice or the shop ships nothing. The safeguard is an idempotency key, a unique ticket on the request so that even if it is sent five times, the money moves exactly once.

**One line to remember:** Payment testing prioritizes money correctness and reliability, declines, timeouts, duplicates, refunds, currency, and especially payment-succeeds-but-confirmation-fails, and idempotency keys matter more than UI validation because retries are routine and only idempotency stops a double charge.

sections.s2_technical:
The success path confirms a valid payment debits the payer, credits the merchant, records a transaction with a unique reference, and returns a confirmed status. Decline cases each produce a specific, safe outcome: insufficient balance must reject without partial debit; an invalid or expired card must be refused before any charge; a wrong CVV must be rejected by the processor. These are financial-correctness cases because the invariant is that a declined payment leaves balances untouched.

Reliability cases are where payments differ most from ordinary forms. A payment timeout means the gateway did not respond in time, so the merchant does not know the outcome; the correct behavior is to treat the result as unknown and reconcile later rather than assuming failure, because the charge may have gone through. A network or callback failure means the asynchronous confirmation webhook did not arrive, so the system must poll or reconcile to discover the true status. The user closing the browser mid-payment must not leave money in limbo; the server-side transaction state is the source of truth, not the browser. The single most critical case is payment-succeeds-but-confirmation-fails: the gateway charged the customer, but the success response or webhook never reached the merchant. If the merchant naively retries the charge, the customer is billed twice; if it marks the order failed, the customer paid for nothing. The only correct design is idempotency plus reconciliation.

Duplicate-transaction handling is the heart of correctness. Because retries happen automatically on timeouts and network blips, the same logical payment can be submitted multiple times. An idempotency key, a unique identifier the client attaches to the payment intent, lets the gateway recognize a repeat and return the original result instead of charging again. The gateway stores the key with the first outcome, so any resend with the same key is a no-op that echoes the first response. Refund cases cover full refunds, which reverse the exact amount, and partial refunds, which reverse part and leave the rest, with the invariant that total refunded never exceeds the captured amount and that refunds are themselves idempotent. Currency conversion cases confirm the correct rate is applied, rounding uses the correct scale with no floating-point error, and the charged and settled currencies are recorded. Transaction-status-mismatch cases confirm that when the merchant's record and the gateway's record disagree, reconciliation resolves to the gateway as the authority on whether money moved.

The reason idempotency and duplicate handling matter more than UI validation is risk asymmetry. A UI validation bug produces an annoying but recoverable user error. A duplicate-charge bug moves real money wrongly, triggers chargebacks, regulatory exposure, and loss of trust, and it happens precisely in the common, unavoidable conditions of timeouts and retries. The senior nuance is that you cannot eliminate retries, so you must make them safe: every mutating payment operation carries an idempotency key, the server deduplicates on that key, and a reconciliation job periodically compares merchant and gateway ledgers to catch and heal any mismatch. Testing therefore must include sending the same idempotency key twice and asserting a single charge, simulating a dropped confirmation and asserting reconciliation converges, and simulating a mid-flight browser close and asserting the server state is authoritative.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — When Priya pays through the National Bank of India gateway, a network blip can cause the client to resend the same payment, and without protection she would be charged twice. This is exactly the idempotency-key and duplicate-handling case.

Problem 2 — Sometimes the bank charges her but the confirmation is lost, so the merchant does not know the payment succeeded. The server-side transaction state must be the source of truth and reconciliation must heal the mismatch. This is exactly the payment-succeeds-but-confirmation-fails case.

Problem 3 — Declines such as insufficient balance, expired card, and wrong CVV must leave balances untouched, and refunds including partial refunds must never exceed the captured amount. These are the financial-correctness invariants.

In the mini-project we model a payment gateway that enforces idempotency, records authoritative transaction state, and supports refunds with the capped-amount invariant, plus a test suite that exercises success, declines, duplicates, lost confirmation, and partial refund. We define a `PaymentResult`, a `PaymentGateway` keyed by idempotency key with declines and refunds, and a `PaymentTestSuite`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Priya's account with two hundred fifty thousand rupees, a good card, and a suite covering success, duplicate, declines, lost confirmation, and partial refund.

Step 1: The success case charges fifty thousand with idempotency key one. The gateway debits the payer, records reference TXN-1 as the authoritative outcome, and returns CAPTURED.

Step 2: The duplicate case resends key one. The gateway sees the key already exists, so it echoes the original result and does not charge again; the balance stays at two hundred thousand, proving idempotency.

Step 3: The decline cases use a fresh gateway each time and confirm an expired card, a wrong CVV, and insufficient balance are all refused with the balance untouched.

Step 4: The lost-confirmation case charges one thousand with key-X, then the client, having never received the confirmation, retries with the same key-X. The gateway recognizes the key and does not double-charge, so the balance drops by exactly one thousand.

Step 5: The partial-refund case captures twenty thousand, refunds five thousand successfully, then attempts to refund twenty thousand more, which would exceed the captured amount and is rejected, proving the refund-cap invariant.

```
  Pay request {idempotencyKey, card, amount}
    │
    ▼
  Key already seen? ──yes──→ ECHO original result (NO second charge)
    │ no
    ▼
  Card expired? ─yes→ DECLINED_CARD (balance unchanged)
  CVV invalid?  ─yes→ DECLINED_CVV  (balance unchanged)
  Insufficient? ─yes→ DECLINED_INSUFFICIENT (balance unchanged)
    │ all no
    ▼
  DEBIT payer → record TXN ref (authoritative) → store by key → CAPTURED
    │
    ├─ confirmation lost → client retries SAME key → echo (single charge)
    ├─ timeout → status UNKNOWN → reconciliation job → heal
    └─ refund(ref, amt) → already+amt <= captured? ─no→ REJECT
                                                    └yes→ REFUNDED (credit payer)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When I test a payment gateway I keep one principle front of mind: this moves real money, so financial correctness and reliability matter far more than cosmetics. My cases start with the success path, a valid payment debits the payer, credits the merchant, records a transaction with a unique reference, and returns captured. Then I cover declines, insufficient balance, invalid or expired card, and wrong CVV, each with the invariant that a declined payment leaves balances completely untouched. Then come the reliability cases that make payments special: a timeout where the result is unknown and must be reconciled rather than assumed failed, a network or callback webhook failure that requires polling or reconciliation, the user closing the browser mid-payment where the server state is authoritative not the browser, and the single most dangerous case, the payment succeeding at the gateway while the confirmation back to the merchant is lost. I also cover duplicate payment requests, full and partial refunds with the invariant that total refunded never exceeds the captured amount, currency conversion with correct rounding and no floating-point error, and transaction-status mismatches where the gateway is the authority on whether money actually moved.

The reason idempotency and duplicate handling matter more than UI validation is risk asymmetry. A UI validation bug is annoying but recoverable; a duplicate-charge bug moves real money wrongly, causes chargebacks and regulatory exposure, and it happens in exactly the routine conditions of timeouts and retries that you cannot eliminate. So the design must make retries safe: every mutating payment carries an idempotency key, the gateway stores the first outcome against that key and returns it unchanged on any resend, and a reconciliation job compares the merchant and gateway ledgers to detect and heal mismatches. My tests therefore send the same key twice and assert a single charge, simulate a dropped confirmation and assert the retry does not double-charge, and assert refunds are capped and idempotent too.

At the National Bank of India I tested exactly this and caught a case where a timeout caused the client to retry without an idempotency key, which would have double-charged customers on slow network days; I made the idempotency key mandatory and added the reconciliation check. Being able to enumerate these money-correctness and reliability cases and to explain why idempotency beats UI validation in importance is what shows an interviewer I understand that in payments the quiet, common failure, charged but not confirmed, is the one that actually loses money and trust.
